name: Omar Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar Olsen, 58, an experienced lineworker after a vocational certificate and apprenticeship. I build and repair power lines, check the meter and write up faults; the pay is low for this trade, but I like fixing the problem in front of me and I use an approved AI assistant every day to sort my notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has the assistant got wrong?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It once swapped Birch East and Birch Extension in a draft report. I caught it against the signed sheet; a tidy sentence is no substitute for a correct feeder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the note assistant is handy, but our hands still have to make the repair and check the meter. A quicker report won't stop a fuse from blowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the tool, yet the quiet future doesn't quiet our rent. I'm an experienced lineworker on the lower pay scale, and a water-heater repair left less than a month's expenses in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking field shifts and use the approved AI assistant each evening to compare my work notes with the safety manual. In the first year my partner Salma and I would stop the paid sports channel and put that money toward rebuilding a small cash reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious at work and tense at home. Our grown children have their own flats, so the rent and the repair bill sit with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the assistant help with yesterday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helped me order notes from a cable fault on Birch Street. I still checked the circuit number in the signed record, because the tool once mixed up two similar feeder names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much did the water heater cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost everything we'd set aside over the summer. Salma's reception shifts at a clinic are part-time, so a thin month is uncomfortable.

I'd remind the crew **meter checks** still need a worker on site.
think: Our **water-heater repair** emptied most of the reserve.
My **lower pay** and Salma's part-time clinic hours make rent stressful.
do: Keep **field shifts** and check approved AI notes against the safety manual each evening.
Cancel the **sports channel** and put that payment into a new cash reserve.
feel: **Curious** at work and tense over the rent.

fieldNote: Omar's **daily AI use** is grounded in safety-manual checks after a feeder-name mistake, not blind trust.
His **baseline anxiety** reflects lower pay, part-time household income and a water-heater repair that depleted savings.

steps.text: Continue paid field shifts while checking AI notes against the manual

Cancel the sports channel and transfer its payment into cash savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot to put dispatchers and line crews in the same room for the route trial. If software saves us a drive, good; if it hides an access warning, we need to know before somebody loses a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical repairs should remain for now, but tighter booking may take away our extra callouts. Salma answers clinic phones, and AI answering customers could also cut her part-time hours in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd volunteer for the approved route trial and keep a log of mismatched feeder names for the dispatcher to review. During the first year Salma and I would postpone visiting our grown daughter across the country if either set of hours drops, and I'd ask the union to request retraining time for clinic and depot staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel energised by a useful trial and anxious about both payslips. We can't buy optimism with a reserve that is almost empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a feeder-name mistake you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen listed Birch East when the outage was on Birch Extension. A dispatcher caught it from a customer's landmark before our truck went to the wrong substation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about the visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown daughter we'll call more often and travel when the budget allows. She is working too, and I won't make her pay for the train.

I'd insist **access warnings** survive the new system.
think: Tighter booking could cut my **extra callouts** on weekend field faults.

do: Join the **approved route trial** and log feeder-name mistakes for dispatch.
Postpone the **daughter visit** if hours fall, and ask the union for paid retraining time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union that thinking AI in 2028 could change Salma's clinic job before robots come for line repairs around 2031. We need published trials and paid places for workers who will inspect the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots can do the field work, and I expect a large cut in our crew hours. Salma's phone shifts might already be gone, our savings are under a month, and there are few nearby utility jobs to chase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union to bargain for paid robot-inspection training and request the company's trial results. In 2029 I'd enroll if wages continue during training; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for inspection vacancies locally and ask the employment office about help reaching jobs farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I stay up calculating rent against two smaller payslips. I can learn the equipment, but I can't promise an employer will need me to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trial result would you read first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for how often a crew had to finish a failed robot repair on a wet line. The glossy success rate means little without the jobs the machine handed back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Salma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Salma we must keep our rent money separate from any course fee. Our grown children can help search listings, but they have bills of their own.

say: I'd name **2028 clinic risk** before 2031 line robots.
I'd ask for **published wet-line trials** and paid inspection places.
think: At **63**, I expect a large cut in field hours.
Salma's **phone shifts** may already be gone while our reserve is nearly empty.
do: Ask the **union** for paid training and published robot trial results.
Enroll in **paid inspection training** if offered in 2029; apply for real jobs and travel help in 2031.
feel: **Sleepless** over two shrinking payslips and rent.
S2.quote: The glossy success rate means little without the jobs the machine handed back.
fieldNote: Omar expects **major crew cuts** at the 2031 robot date and says he stays awake calculating household rent.
His **paid training** condition and request for trial failure data ground his interest in technology in actual wages and safety.

steps.text: Ask the union for paid training and published robot failure data
Enrol in robot-inspection training in 2029 if wages continue
Apply for posted local inspection jobs when robots arrive
Ask the employment office for travel help to distant vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years gives us a chance to test robots on real faults and bargain over the work left for people. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I might retire, but our thin savings make that a guess until I see the pension statement. Salma's clinic phone job could shrink in 2031, three years before a robot touches my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask payroll for a written pension estimate and join any union safety group testing field robots. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection placement if it exists; during the first robot year I'd compare the posted inspection pay with retirement income before choosing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more capable with extra time, but not secure. A longer runway doesn't put rent money in our account today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test with the group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Birch Extension feeder has a label that looks like Birch East in poor light. I'd want the robot to stop and call for a human check instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the placement never opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep safe paid line shifts while they exist and ask the union for the actual staffing plan. I won't walk away from wages for a training promise with no start date.

say: I'd seek **real-fault trials** and negotiated work before 2034 robots.
I'd separate **2031 thinking AI** from later field machines.
think: Retirement at **66** needs a written pension figure.
Salma's **clinic hours** may shrink in 2031 while rent is due now.
do: Request a **pension estimate** and join a union robot safety group this month.
Take a **paid placement** if offered in 2032; compare posted inspection pay with retirement income in 2034.
S3.quote: A longer runway doesn't put rent money in our account today.
fieldNote: Omar's **2034 choice** requires actual pension and inspection pay figures, with Salma's earlier clinic risk in the household budget.
His **robot trial criterion** is whether the machine stops at a confusing label rather than guessing at a feeder.

steps.text: Request a written pension estimate before choosing retirement
Join the union robot safety group and test confusing feeder labels
Take a paid inspection placement in 2032 if one opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger lineworkers ten years is long enough to record every odd circuit and insist on public safety results. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and repair robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be retired by 71 if the pension and Salma's income cover rent, but neither figure is certain yet. The water-heater bill and low balance are real now, so I can't call this an easy picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid line shifts, clear the heater debt and request pension records for both of us. In 2037 we'd choose a retirement date only if a low-hours budget covers rent; if it doesn't, I'd apply for paid inspection work before robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed by the robot date and still anxious about money next month. A decade gives me time to try the tools, but not permission to forget the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you save during those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the heater balance is cleared, I'd transfer fifteen from each real weekend callout to a reserve. I won't put a pretend overtime figure into our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave the next crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave a marked photograph of the Birch Extension label and the dispatcher note that caught the mistake. A trainee should know why the names are easily confused.

say: I'd call for **public safety results** and clear circuit records.
I'd note **2039 repair robots** arrive when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement at **71** needs verified pension and household income.
Our **heater debt** and low balance still cause immediate pressure.
do: Keep **paid shifts**, clear heater debt and request pension records.
Save **fifteen from real callouts** after the debt clears, then assess retirement or inspection work in 2037.
feel: **Less pressed** by robots, still anxious about next month's money.
S4.quote: I won't put a pretend overtime figure into our plan.
fieldNote: Omar's **long preparation window** cannot erase the current heater debt or uncertainty in Salma's hours.
His **conditional saving** uses real weekend callouts only after the debt is cleared, keeping the retirement budget honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Salma's clinic phone work could shrink first, then robots could cut my field hours in 2031. Paid inspection training, published failure data, real jobs and travel help would let us act before rent is due.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the crew when the robot stops in the rain and hands the fault back. A success chart won't cover the rent if people lose paid shifts.

headlineQuote: A success chart won't cover the rent if people lose paid shifts.
portrait: Omar is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, lower pay and less than one month saved.
His **water-heater debt** and Salma's part-time clinic hours keep AI Plateau financially tense despite stable field tasks.
He uses **AI every day** for notes and route trials while checking feeder names against signed records.
The **2031 robot date** alarms him because he expects major crew-hour losses after Salma's phone work may shrink.
A longer runway allows **pension checks** from real callouts, while he keeps paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Omar most because Salma's clinic work may shrink before robots cut his field hours.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **paid training**, published robot failure data, real vacancies and help reaching distant work.
